title: ADRs & Roadmapping
description: A preview of the Planning & Communication toolkit's decision and narrative artifacts.
body: Named artifacts this page previews What a good ADR contains When a decision needs an ADR Roadmaps for two different audiences The business case, stripped to what gets funded ADR conventions that keep the practice alive A worked roadmap example ADR template Four specific templates, not just the general practice below. Architecture Decision Record Template, a durable format for hard-to-reverse decisions plus the conventions that keep the practice alive rather than decorative Target-State Narrative Template, a prose-first structure for describing a future operating model to executive audiences, built on the idea that diagrams illustrate but shouldn't replace clear writing Capability-Driven Roadmap Method, building multi-year roadmaps rooted in capability gaps rather than technology initiatives, with traceability from strategy to initiative Business Case Template and Narrative, a financial model paired with the narrative structure that makes it defensible to executives and finance reviewers, including an honest options analysis and named benefit owners An Architecture Decision Record exists to answer one question well after the fact: why did we decide this, given what we knew at the time. Most ADR templates fail at exactly that. Not every choice. Writing one for every minor decision produces the same fatigue problem as over-gating architecture review. When the decision is expensive to reverse, when it affects more than one team, or when you can already predict someone will ask "why did we do it this way" in six months. What counts as expensive to reverse scales with the team, a change that's a quick fix for a three-person startup might be a multi-quarter migration for a five-hundred-engineer org, so weigh it against your own team's actual capacity, not a fixed unit of time. Reversible implementation choices scoped entirely within one team, where the cost of writing the record exceeds the cost of just trying something and changing it later if it's wrong. The single most common roadmap mistake: one document trying to serve both an engineering audience and a business audience, serving neither well. Organized by system or capability, includes technical sequencing dependencies, appropriately detailed about implementation approach, timeframes expressed as sprints or quarters. Organized by customer or business outcome, no implementation detail, timeframes expressed as calendar dates tied to business events (a renewal cycle, a fiscal year), directly reusable in the board reporting format described on the Board Reporting page. What separates a business case that gets approved from one that gets deferred indefinitely. A specific, falsifiable claim (this reduces X by Y amount, measured how, by when) tied to a number the approver already tracks, with the cost of not doing it stated as explicitly as the cost of doing it. A business case built entirely around technical merit ("this reduces technical debt") with no connection to a business metric anyone outside engineering tracks. Technical merit is necessary justification, rarely sufficient justification on its own. The template is the easy part. These conventions are what turn a folder of documents into a resource people consult. Numbers are never reused, even for deprecated or superseded ADRs. The number is an identifier, not a priority. Once accepted, the decision is immutable. Circumstances change, a new ADR supersedes it. Editing the original to reflect current understanding destroys the record. One decision per ADR. A compound ADR is a sign the team is avoiding the harder work of separating decisions. One to two pages. Longer usually means design work leaking in that belongs elsewhere; shorter usually means the alternatives section is missing. Author by role, not just name. "Lead Architect, Payments" carries context that survives staff changes. A compressed real example showing the method end to end: strategic priority through capability gaps through sequenced initiatives. Strategic priority: reduce customer acquisition cost 25 percent within 36 months while maintaining conversion on qualified leads. A ready-to-use starting point for the format described above: context, decision, alternatives considered, consequences. Markdown for pasting into your own docs system, or a formatted Word doc.

title: Agile and SAFe
body: The four values, and what commonly gets installed instead Why "doing agile" and "being agile" diverge Where SAFe helps Where SAFe becomes its own theater Scaling down deliberately, not just up Signs agile or SAFe has become theater Each value in the agile manifesto requires something real. Most organizations install a process substitute that satisfies the ritual without the underlying substance. The gap that determines whether the ceremonies are earning their keep. The team changes what it does based on what it learns, mid-sprint if warranted, and treats each ceremony as a tool it owns and can modify or drop the moment it stops earning its keep. Standup, retro, planning, and review run on schedule regardless of whether they're producing value, treated as compliance requirements rather than tools the team controls. The tell: ask when the team last changed its own process based on a retro, and get silence. A real coordination problem exists at scale, and SAFe was built to address it, whatever else gets said about the framework. Coordinating dependencies across many teams building toward a shared release or shared platform, where informal coordination breaks down past a certain team count and someone has to own cross-team sequencing explicitly rather than leaving it to hope. Often cited around 50 to 125 people, five to twelve teams, though the real trigger is dependency density between teams, not headcount alone. Ten independent teams with no shared release need none of this; four teams shipping one product together might. The same framework, installed for a coordination problem the organization doesn't have. The framework's ceremonies, PI planning, the various sync meetings, the layered roles, get installed wholesale regardless of whether the organization's actual coordination problem matches what SAFe was built to solve, producing ceremony overhead that outweighs the coordination it buys. Ask what specific coordination failure a given SAFe ceremony prevents. If the honest answer is "we don't know, this is just what SAFe says to do," the ceremony is cargo cult, not a solution to a problem the organization has. The adoption decision most organizations skip: choosing which pieces to install and which to leave out. Apply only the specific mechanisms that address a genuine, named coordination problem, and skip the rest. A framework adopted partially and deliberately produces less overhead than either the full framework or no coordination structure at all. Adopting the framework "properly" because partial adoption feels like doing it wrong, which installs overhead for coordination problems the organization doesn't have, simply because the framework bundles them together with the ones it does. Patterns that show up when process is running on schedule but no longer producing what it's meant to. Ceremonies run on schedule regardless of whether the team can name what each one is currently producing The team has never changed its own process based on a retrospective Story points or velocity get reported upward as if comparable across different teams SAFe ceremonies are followed without anyone able to name the specific coordination failure each one prevents "Being agile" and "following the ceremony calendar" are treated as the same thing by leadership

title: AI and the Engineering Operating Model
body: What changes, and what doesn't AI productivity does not automatically equal more story points Code review changes shape What happens to junior engineer development Measuring productivity when the tool is part of the output Signs AI adoption is being measured or managed naively AI-assisted coding shifts specific parts of the job. It doesn't touch others, and treating it as a uniform speedup misreads what's happening. The most common measurement mistake, and the one most likely to produce a plan that breaks on contact with reality. AI-assisted coding speeds up the mechanical parts, boilerplate, first drafts, syntax, which shifts the real bottleneck to review, architectural judgment, and testing: the parts that were never the slow part for a senior engineer, but were close to the entire job for a junior one. Treating a rise in lines of code or pull request volume as productivity, then setting headcount or delivery expectations against that number. The plan breaks the moment the team hits the bottleneck AI never touched: review capacity and architectural decision-making. Reviewing AI-generated code is a different skill than reviewing human-written code, and most engineers were never trained on the difference. Reviewing AI-generated code means checking for plausible-but-wrong patterns, code that looks idiomatic and compiles cleanly but embeds a subtly incorrect assumption, more than checking for the kind of mistake a human engineer is likely to make. That's a distinct reviewing skill. Review fatigue from higher volume, combined with AI-generated code's tendency to look confident and clean, produces a false sense of safety. Reviewers approve faster because the code reads well, not because they verified it more rigorously. The concern worth stating honestly, and the one most tempting to dismiss because it doesn't show up as a problem until much later. A junior engineer who leans on AI for the mechanical work skips the repetition that used to build pattern recognition and debugging intuition the slow way. That intuition doesn't obviously appear missing until a novel problem requires it and it isn't there. Deliberately assign some work without AI assistance specifically for skill-building, framed as a training decision rather than a productivity one, the same way a pilot still trains on manual flight even though autopilot handles most of the actual flying. The measurement question every other section on this page eventually points back to. Raw output volume: lines of code, pull requests merged, AI suggestions accepted. All of these can rise while the team ships less real, correct, maintained value, since none of them measure whether the output was right. The outcome measures already covered on Engineering Metrics, cycle time, change failure rate, and ultimately business outcomes, tracked specifically before and after AI tooling adoption, rather than assuming adoption itself is automatically the win. Patterns that show up when AI tooling gets adopted enthusiastically but without adjusting how the organization measures or trains around it. Productivity claims rest on lines of code, PR volume, or AI suggestion acceptance rate rather than outcome measures Code review practice hasn't been adjusted for the specific failure modes of AI-generated code No deliberate mechanism exists for junior engineers to build skills without AI assistance Change failure rate or defect rate hasn't been tracked before and after AI tooling adoption Headcount or timeline plans assume a productivity multiplier that was asserted rather than measured

title: AI FinOps Map
description: Cost modeling stage by stage across AWS, Azure, GCP, OCI, and self-hosted, the same environments the Architecture Map covers in depth.
body: Pricing model: tokens vs amortized hardware Find your own break-even point Reserved capacity vs GPU procurement Chargeback & unit economics Cost observability & budget alerting Model selection as a cost lever Waste: idle reservations and orphaned capacity Prompt caching Batch / asynchronous processing The fundamental cost shape differs before any workload-specific decisions get made. Bedrock is billed per token, input and output priced separately, output typically several times more expensive than input, with per-model rates spanning roughly $0.035 to $10 per million input tokens depending on model tier. Cost scales directly and immediately with usage, unpredictable at the account level until volume stabilizes. Pay-as-you-go is billed per token, input and output priced separately, output typically several times more expensive than input. Cost scales directly and immediately with usage, visible per-call, but unpredictable at the account level until volume stabilizes. Vertex AI bills per character for most Gemini models rather than per token, input and output metered separately. A real, easy-to-miss cost multiplier here: Gemini's internal reasoning tokens are billed as output, and can inflate a request's real cost five to tenfold beyond what the visible response length would suggest. On-demand OCI Generative AI is billed per transaction (character-based) for on-demand inference, separate from the per-unit-hour rate that applies once you move to a dedicated cluster. Consumption draws against an existing Universal Credits commitment rather than a standalone bill. Cost is amortized GPU time (purchase or lease depreciation, power, cooling, ops staff), largely fixed regardless of query volume until you hit a capacity ceiling and need to add hardware. Marginal cost per additional query approaches zero until that ceiling, then jumps in a large step when you provision another node. The formula above, made concrete. Runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent anywhere or stored. Committing ahead of time to guarantee throughput and control cost variance. Provisioned Throughput reserves dedicated capacity in model units, billed hourly whether used or not, at roughly $24 to $200 per hour depending on model. Only pays off above sustained utilization; buying a 6-month commitment before traffic is stable is the single fastest way to overspend here. Custom or fine-tuned models require Provisioned Throughput; they can't run on-demand at all. Provisioned Throughput Units (PTU) reserve dedicated capacity at a flat monthly rate, converting variable token cost into a predictable fixed cost, but only pays off above a specific utilization threshold; idle PTU capacity is money spent on nothing. Provisioned throughput, priced per generative scale unit hour rather than per token, with 20 to 45 percent savings available via 1-month or 1-year commitments. Break-even against on-demand typically lands around $50 a day in sustained spend on a single model; below that, on-demand usually wins. Dedicated AI clusters bill per unit-hour, but the distinctive gotcha here is the minimum commitment: hosting clusters require at least 744 unit-hours, roughly a full month, even if actual usage is far lower. That minimum doesn't exist on the other three clouds' reserved-capacity tiers. Owning or leasing GPUs is the hardware equivalent of a reserved-capacity commitment: a large fixed cost that only pays off at sustained utilization. Renting from a GPU cloud (on-demand) is the hardware equivalent of pay-as-you-go, more expensive per hour but no idle-capacity risk. Making AI spend attributable to the team or product that generated it, not a single opaque line item. Cost Explorer's tagging and cost allocation tags attribute Bedrock spend to a team, product, or environment tag, feeding a per-team chargeback model the same way any other AWS resource would. Cost Management's tagging and scope hierarchy lets you attribute Foundry deployment spend to a subscription, resource group, or tag, feeding a per-team or per-product chargeback model the same way any other Azure resource would. Cloud Billing labels plus BigQuery billing export let you attribute Vertex AI spend down to the label or project level, queryable alongside the rest of the GCP bill rather than as an isolated line item. Compartment structure plus tag-based attribution in OCI Cost Analysis, with FOCUS 1.2 exports increasingly the default pipeline for feeding a chargeback model, falls back to a tagless mode when tag coverage is incomplete. No managed billing hierarchy to lean on; attribution requires your own request-tagging at the application layer (which team or product initiated the call) correlated against GPU-hour cost allocated proportionally to usage. This is meaningfully more engineering work to build. Catching a cost anomaly (a runaway agent loop, a misconfigured retry, a prompt that ballooned in size) before the monthly bill does. AWS Budgets with configurable thresholds and Cost Anomaly Detection using machine learning to flag unusual spend patterns automatically, without a manually defined rule for every scenario. Cost Management budgets with action-group-triggered alerts at defined thresholds; Monitor can alert on token consumption rate directly if instrumented, catching an anomaly within the billing period rather than after it closes. Budgets & Alerts plus Cost Anomaly Detection at the billing-account level; the reasoning-token cost multiplier from Stage 1 is exactly the kind of anomaly this catches before it compounds across a month of traffic. OCI Cost Analysis with budget-based alerts, increasingly paired with FOCUS 1.2 billing exports for teams that have moved off the native dashboard onto a broader FinOps pipeline. No native billing-anomaly alerting since there's no per-token bill to watch. The equivalent signal is GPU utilization and request-rate anomalies via Prometheus alerting, an unusual spike in request volume or output length is the leading indicator y

title: AI Governance Map
description: Four layers, from data foundation to responsible AI oversight, each with concrete controls mapped to what breaks without them and which regulatory frameworks.
body: Data foundation Governance layer Trusted outputs Responsible AI & high-risk oversight Model risk management The standards and credentials landscape Is ISO 42001 certification worth pursuing Regulatory framework mapping Accountability & audit trail AI-specific incident response Before anything else, know what the model uses. If you cannot answer where a piece of training or retrieval data came from, nothing above this layer holds up. Source registry covering every system feeding the AI pipeline Data dictionary defining what each field means and where it originated Lineage and provenance tracking from source document to retrieved chunk Clear data ownership assigned per source system, not left implicit NIST AI RMF's Map function starts here: you cannot assess risk in a system whose inputs you cannot trace. Without this layer, an incident investigation cannot answer "where did this bad output come from," which is usually the first question an investigation asks. Once the data foundation is solid, decide who decides what. Definition locks, retrieval boundaries, input validation, and a named data steward give the system clear lines of accountability. Definition locks: agreed, versioned definitions for terms the system reasons about, not left to drift between teams Retrieval boundaries: which sources an agent or index is allowed to draw from for a given use case Input validation on both user prompts and any document entering the ingestion pipeline A named data steward with actual authority to change what's retrievable Without a data steward, retrieval boundaries erode silently as new sources get connected for convenience, and the system starts answering from data nobody approved for that use case. This is the layer that turns "we have a RAG pipeline" into "we have a RAG pipeline someone is accountable for." With governance in place, you can start defending your answers. Confidence thresholds, output guardrails, and bias checks turn "the AI said so" into something you can stand behind to a customer, auditor, or regulator. Confidence thresholds tied to the human-in-the-loop tiering model (see the Architecture Map) Output guardrails: schema validation, citation requirements, forbidden-content checks before a response ships Bias and fairness checks on outputs for any use case touching people (hiring, credit, care recommendations) Explainability sufficient to answer "why did it say that" after the fact, not just at design time A confidence score without a documented threshold policy is not a control, it's a number nobody acts on consistently. This layer is what regulators and auditors ask to see evidence of; it needs to produce artifacts (logs, rubric scores), not just exist as a design intention. The outer layer: autonomous agents, high-risk decisions, and regulated use cases. This only works because everything underneath it is already solid. Formal classification of which use cases count as high-risk under applicable frameworks Documented incident response plan specific to AI failures, not a generic IT incident process Human oversight for high-risk decisions, implemented as the Tier 2 gate described on the Architecture Map, not a policy statement with no technical enforcement Hallucination and groundedness checks running continuously, not only at initial launch Credit scoring, employment screening, and medical decisioning fall within the EU AI Act's Annex III high-risk use cases when the specific system matches the listed criteria there, not automatically because it operates in one of those domains generally. Article 14 requires human oversight for systems that do qualify. Enforcement timelines for specific Annex III obligations have shifted since the Act's original schedule, some employment-related obligations were pushed from August 2026 to December 2027 under a later political agreement, so confirm the current applicable date for your specific use case rather than assuming a fixed 2026 deadline. Treating the model itself, not just its outputs, as something with a lifecycle that needs governing. A model inventory listing every deployed model, its version, what it's used for, and who owns the decision to keep using it. Pre-deployment evaluation against a defined rubric before a new model version replaces an old one. Ongoing drift monitoring in production, tied to the observability stage on the Architecture Map, not a one-time evaluation at launch. The single most common gap: a team can name the model they deployed in January but not confirm what's running in production today after three silent provider-side updates. If you cannot answer "which exact model version produced this output," you cannot investigate an incident or defend a decision. Four different things people mean when they say "AI governance," easy to conflate and different in what they certify, who holds them, and what they cost. A real decision with a real cost, not something to default into because the standard exists. Enterprise customers or regulators are asking for independent evidence of AI governance maturity, not just a policy document. Selling into procurement processes where a competitor's ISO 42001 badge is becoming a checkbox. The organization already holds ISO 27001, since the incremental cost and timeline drop substantially when the management-system muscle already exists. A small AI footprint with a handful of internal use cases and no customer demanding third-party evidence. The four layers above aren't solidly in place yet, certifying a management system before the underlying technical controls exist produces a certificate that doesn't reflect reality, and an auditor will eventually find that gap. NIST AI RMF, applied honestly and evidenced internally, covers most of the same ground without the $20,000 to $60,000 audit cost and multi-year commitment. Which control layer above satisfies which framework's requirement. Not legal advice; confirm applicability with counsel for your specific use case and jurisdiction. Who

title: AI Portfolio Management
description: Which AI initiatives should get built, scored and classified with the same discipline applied to the rest of the application estate.
body: Scoring dimensions and classification Feasibility and data readiness gate the score, they don't just contribute to it Reversibility deserves its own weight Kill criteria set before the bet starts Score an initiative Signs AI portfolio governance isn't real Nine dimensions feed the score; four classifications follow from it. The point isn't precision, it's forcing the same questions to be asked of every initiative rather than letting the loudest pitch skip the screen entirely. Averaging all nine dimensions into one number lets a high-value, technically infeasible idea pass through if it scores generously elsewhere. Screen on feasibility and data readiness first. If the data doesn't exist at usable quality, or the model risk is unacceptable regardless of upside, the initiative doesn't reach a business-value conversation at all. Gating dimensions eliminate; they don't get averaged away. A compelling business case with a fatal data gap can still produce a respectable average score if the other eight dimensions are strong, which is exactly how organizations end up funding pilots that were never going to work, discovered only after real money and credibility were spent. Not all AI bets carry the same downside if they fail, and the classification should reflect that. A pilot built on a vendor API is cheap to unwind. A model embedded into a core workflow customers now depend on is not. Two initiatives with identical business-value scores warrant different treatment if one is trivially reversible and the other isn't. Treating an irreversible bet with the same enthusiasm as a reversible pilot because both scored well on value, without ever separately asking what it costs to walk away if the initial results don't hold up at scale. AI initiatives are unusually prone to surviving on prestige rather than results, which makes advance kill criteria more important here than almost anywhere else in the portfolio. Define, before funding, the specific result that would trigger a move to Watch or Kill, a metric, a threshold, a date. Write it down where it can't be quietly renegotiated once the team is emotionally invested in the outcome. An initiative that's been "six months from proving itself" for over a year, kept alive because killing an AI project carries a different kind of organizational embarrassment than killing an ordinary feature, independent of what the actual results show. Score all nine dimensions 1 to 5. Feasibility and data readiness are hard gates, a low score on either kills the initiative regardless of everything else. Runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent anywhere or stored. Patterns that show up when AI initiatives are being funded by momentum rather than by the same discipline applied elsewhere in the technology portfolio. No AI initiative has ever been formally moved to Kill despite some producing no measurable result Feasibility and data readiness were never checked before funding, only the business case The same initiative has been described as close to proving itself for well over a year No one can name what's currently in Watch status or when it's due for reassessment AI investment decisions bypass the standard capital allocation process applied to everything else

title: Application Portfolio Management
body: What exists behind this preview The Gartner TIME model, applied Risk as an independent axis, not a TIME input Turning individual scores into a portfolio signal TIME quadrant classifier A working spreadsheet instrument, not a static framework: three linked sheets feeding one dashboard, with the same scoring logic reused for standing portfolio governance and for scoring an acquisition target's stack under diligence. 3 linked sheets · 1 live dashboard · standing portfolio and M&A variants Every known debt item scored on severity, business impact, confidence, and remediation effort, rolled up to a priority ranking. Direct remediation, annual carry, and contingent risk cost per item, each carrying its own confidence rating Status and aging tracked against a target remediation window, so stale items surface instead of hiding Rolls into portfolio-level totals: active items by severity, cost by confidence tier, overdue count A five-factor risk score per application, independent of how valuable or well-built the system is. Cybersecurity, compliance, operational resilience, vendor, and knowledge-concentration risk scored separately, then composited Surfaces the application that's fine on paper but one departure or one vendor lapse from a bad quarter Every application placed on the Gartner TIME grid using a Business Value score and a Technical Health score. Business Value built from five factors: strategic alignment, business criticality, user reach, differentiation, regulatory necessity Technical Health built from five factors: technology currency, architecture quality, integration complexity, data architecture fit, technical debt Composite Portfolio Score, cost score, and risk score sit alongside the classification as informational overlays, not inputs to it The same instrument, repointed at a target company's application estate during diligence or the first 100 days. Same scoring mechanics, framed around acquisition-specific questions: what's redundant with the acquirer's stack, what's a hidden Eliminate candidate the seller never flagged Feeds directly into the Integration Architecture Decision Tree's merge, integrate, or coexist call per system Every application lands in one of four quadrants based on two independent scores: how much the business needs it, and how healthy it is technically. Invest: high value, high health — fund it. Tolerate: low value, high health — leave it alone, don't over-invest. Migrate: high value, low health — the modernization backlog, ranked by value at risk. Eliminate: low value, low health — the retirement candidates most portfolios are carrying more of than anyone admits. Business Value gets inflated when the scorer is the system's own owner. Score it with someone outside the owning team in the room, or the whole portfolio drifts toward Invest and the model stops doing its job. Technical Health is the opposite failure: engineers score their own systems harshly relative to peers they haven't had to maintain, which skews Migrate counts up. A system can be a clean Invest on the TIME grid and still be the one that takes the company down. Risk is scored and reported separately on purpose. Folding risk into Technical Health hides exactly the applications that need visibility: strategically critical, well-funded, actively developed, and sitting on a single unreplaceable engineer or an end-of-life dependency no one has scheduled work against. Reporting risk on its own axis keeps that combination visible instead of averaging it away. These get remediation budget ahead of Migrate-quadrant systems, even though they score well overall, because the downside is asymmetric: a breach or a key-person departure on a high-value system costs more than slow modernization debt on a low-value one. One application's score is a data point. The value is in the aggregate: how many Eliminate candidates are still costing real money, how concentrated the high-risk applications are, whether Migrate is growing or shrinking quarter over quarter. Average Composite Portfolio Score by quadrant, count of high-risk applications, count of high-cost applications relative to their Business Value, and the ratio of Eliminate-classified applications still consuming a meaningful share of total run cost. Movement in these over two or three quarters tells you whether governance is changing behavior or just producing a nicer chart. Treating this as a one-time inventory exercise. A TIME classification from eighteen months ago is closer to fiction than data; technical health decays continuously even when business value hasn't moved, so the cadence matters as much as the scoring model itself. Score one application on the same five-factor Business Value and Technical Health axes the full instrument uses. Runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent anywhere or stored. Risk and cost scoring, and the multi-application portfolio view, are part of the full simulator.

title: Architecture Principles Library
body: What makes a principle worth having Buy before build, build only where differentiation justifies the cost Pay down technical debt continuously, not in campaigns Make reversible decisions quickly; reserve slow deliberation for the irreversible Prefer loose coupling between autonomous teams over tight integration Failure is the default state; design for it Observability is a first-class concern, not an afterthought Prefer convention over configuration; prefer explicit over implicit Automate what gets done more than twice Data has an authoritative source; other copies are derived, not parallel Data models reflect domain reality, not system convenience Classify data by sensitivity before any other decision The team that builds runs, or the runbook doesn't exist Decisions are recorded; rationale is part of the decision Small, stable teams outperform large, dynamic ones for complex work Measure what matters; do not optimize what is merely easy to measure Conflict is a feature, not a bug Most architecture principles are bad: generic ("we will be agile"), self-serving ("we prefer our favorite technology"), or untestable ("we will deliver business value"). A useful principle has four properties. Names a specific trade-off the organization has chosen Is defensible against its opposite Produces different decisions than its absence would Comes with examples of when it was applied and what was given up as a result Rationale: Most software the organization needs has already been built by someone else. Building it again produces ongoing maintenance costs for software that doesn't differentiate the business. Trade-off: Loss of control over roadmap and feature set. Accepted for commodity capabilities, rejected for differentiating ones. Worked example: Customer identity management is commodity, adopt a commercial platform. Fraud detection for a specific transaction pattern is differentiating, build it. Signs of misapplication: Everything gets classified as differentiating to justify building. The cure is making someone name the differentiation concretely. Rationale: Debt accumulates continuously. Campaigns to address it are always disruptive, under-scoped, and insufficient. Trade-off: Feature velocity appears lower in the short term because capacity is visibly allocated away from new work. Worked example: Delivery teams allocate 15 to 20 percent of sprint capacity to debt items, owned by engineering, informed to product. Signs of misapplication: The allocation becomes theoretical; sprint reviews consistently show 100 percent feature work. Rationale: Treating all decisions with the same process produces either dangerous speed on the irreversible or pointless bureaucracy on the reversible. Trade-off: Some decisions are harder to classify than the principle implies; the organization has to develop judgment about what's reversible in its context. Worked example: A logging library choice is reversible, the team picks and moves. A primary data platform is not reversible within a reasonable timeframe, it goes through review with ADR documentation. Signs of misapplication: Teams classify inconvenient decisions as irreversible to defer them, or reversible to avoid oversight. The test: what does it cost in time and money to change this in 18 months? Rationale: Tight coupling between systems produces tight coupling between the teams that own them, and destroys both the system's and the team's autonomy over time. Trade-off: Loose coupling costs more to build initially; interfaces take design effort that a shared database doesn't. Worked example: The Order team calls the Customer service's API rather than reading the Customer database directly. The Customer team can refactor storage without coordinating with Order. Signs of misapplication: Teams paper over coupling with facades that still expose the underlying structure. Test: if the upstream team changes its implementation, does the downstream code break? Rationale: At any non-trivial scale, something is always failing. Systems designed assuming components work experience their first real failure as an outage. Trade-off: Upfront complexity; designing for failure takes real thought and adds code paths. Worked example: The order placement service, when the fraud service is unavailable, falls back to rule-based scoring rather than refusing orders. Flagged orders get deferred review. Signs of misapplication: Retries and fallbacks added without thinking through cascade effects; retry storms that take down dependencies are worse than the original failure. Rationale: Systems not designed to be observed are systems whose behavior is a mystery in production, and the cost of instrumenting retroactively is higher than instrumenting from the start. Trade-off: Instrumentation is real code that must be maintained; noisy instrumentation is worse than none. Worked example: Every service produces request logs with correlation IDs, metrics on the operations that matter most, and traces covering cross-service flows, specified alongside functional requirements. Signs of misapplication: Teams log everything, measure nothing, and produce dashboards nobody reads. The cure: for each piece of instrumentation, ask what decision it supports. Rationale: Configuration without convention produces infinite surface area. Convention without explicit seams produces invisible magic. Trade-off: The organization must invest in establishing and evolving conventions, ongoing work that drifts into inconsistency without it. Worked example: All services log in a common format and expose health/metrics on conventional paths. A service deviating for regulatory reasons documents why, explicitly. Signs of misapplication: Conventions are stated but not enforced; new services do whatever their authors prefer. Rationale: Manual work is error-prone, non-repeatable, and invisible. title: Architecture Review Board
body: What belongs in front of the board, and what doesn't Evidence over drawings Setting it up: composition and authority The review itself Running it long-term without decaying into theater Empty slots: turn them into innovation salons, not canceled meetings Signs the board has become theater The most common way a review board fails is reviewing everything, which turns it into a bottleneck and trains teams to route around it. The same filter used to decide when a decision needs an ADR applies here. The distinction that separates a review with teeth from a rubber stamp with a diagram attached. The actual running system, real traffic patterns, real incident history, a working prototype or spike, existing code. Evidence that was produced by doing the engineering work, not evidence produced to satisfy the meeting. A polished architecture diagram produced in the days before the review, disconnected from the actual codebase, that nobody consults again once the meeting ends. The tell: check the diagram file's last-modified date six months later. If it's the review date, it was never a working artifact. Two decisions made once, at founding, that determine whether the board has real standing or just a name. A small standing group, four to six people, spanning the systems most likely to be affected by cross-cutting decisions. Rotate membership on a defined cycle so it doesn't calcify into the same five people's opinions indefinitely. The proposing team's own senior engineer is always in the room, never reviewed in absentia. See Technology Decision Rights: the board should be Consulted, rarely Accountable. A named individual, the CTO or a delegate, is accountable for architecture standards and can be persuaded by a strong board recommendation, but the board's vote is input, not a decision no one can override. What makes a specific session evidence-based rather than theater, independent of how well the board was set up. The proposing team walks through the actual tradeoffs they considered and rejected, the same alternatives-considered discipline covered on the ADR page, with real numbers behind claims (this handles X load, this costs Y) rather than assertions. The review produces a decision and its reasoning captured in an ADR, not a verbal thumbs-up that disappears when the meeting ends. The review becomes a presentation the team already knows how to pass: confident language and a clean diagram calibrated to satisfy the audience rather than stress-test the reasoning. At that point the board is a rubber stamp with theater added, arguably worse than no review, since it spends real time producing a false signal of scrutiny. A board that works well in its first year and quietly stops working in its third is the most common lifecycle, and it's predictable enough to design against. A standing cadence, biweekly is common, that runs whether or not there's a full docket. A public backlog of upcoming reviews so teams plan around it instead of being surprised. Periodic retrospectives on the board's own past decisions: did what it approved work out, was what it blocked right to block. The board approves the same rubber-stamp pattern for months. Membership never rotates, so the room's authority rests on tenure rather than current context. No one checks whether a past decision held up, so the board never learns whether its own judgment is any good, and keeps operating on the same instincts regardless of outcomes. What to do with a scheduled review slot that has nothing queued for it, which happens regularly once a board is running well and teams aren't manufacturing proposals just to fill the docket. Instead of canceling the slot, which trains people to deprioritize the cadence, or filling it with a low-stakes item just to have something on the agenda, open it up: anyone can bring an early-stage idea, a technical curiosity, or a "here's something I've been thinking about" for informal discussion. No funding decision required, no ADR required, just structured space for ideas that aren't ready for a formal pitch yet. It keeps the room's habit and rhythm intact, the same people, the same regular slot, the same expectation of showing up prepared to think carefully, without wasting the time when nothing formal needs review. It also creates a low-stakes on-ramp: an idea that gets genuine interest in a salon session is exactly the kind of thing ready to become a real pitch at the next innovation tournament. Patterns that show up when a review board exists on the calendar but isn't functioning as a real forcing function anymore. Reviews consistently approve with no real pushback or requested changes No one can name a decision the board changed its mind about after seeing how it played out Board membership hasn't rotated in over a year Decisions aren't captured anywhere durable, no ADR, no written record, once the meeting ends Teams prepare a specific "board-ready" version of their architecture that differs from what's running in production

title: Board Reporting
description: A preview of the Technology Board Reporting Framework: what works reporting technology, security, and AI posture to a board.
body: Cadence & format The out-of-cycle escalation path Two clocks, not one: internal escalation versus external disclosure Translating technical risk into business risk Investment & roadmap tied to outcomes Security & compliance posture Reporting on AI specifically Common mistakes, named directly Sample board deck How often the board hears from technology, and in what form, before a single word of content is decided. A consistent one-page technology summary attached to every board meeting, regardless of whether anything dramatic happened, plus a deeper technology review quarterly or semi-annually. Consistency builds the board's pattern recognition for what normal looks like, so they notice when something isn't. Technology only showing up on the agenda when something has gone wrong. This trains the board to associate a CTO presentation with bad news, which makes every appearance feel like a confession rather than a normal operating rhythm. The specific mechanism that makes a promise like "the quarterly report never contains a surprise" true, rather than aspirational. A pre-agreed threshold for what triggers a call to the board chair or committee lead outside the normal cadence, a confirmed material breach, a regulatory filing obligation, a decision that can't wait until the next scheduled meeting, defined before an incident happens, not improvised during one. No defined threshold, which means every incident becomes a judgment call about whether it's board-worthy, made under pressure by whoever's closest to it. That's how a material issue ends up sitting until the next quarterly meeting for no reason other than nobody decided to escalate it sooner. For a public company, the out-of-cycle path above and the regulatory disclosure deadline are related but distinct, and conflating them is a real risk, not just an organizational nicety. The board should hear about a likely-material incident within roughly 24 hours, well ahead of any external deadline, so there's time to prepare a proper disclosure and align on the facts before anyone outside the company sees them. Under current SEC rules, a public company must disclose a cybersecurity incident determined to be material on Form 8-K within four business days of that materiality determination, not four days from discovery. The clock starts when materiality is decided, which is exactly why the internal escalation path needs to run well ahead of it, not up against it. The single most common failure mode in board reporting: reporting the risk in the language it was diagnosed in, not the language the board makes decisions in. "A vulnerability in our authentication system could allow unauthorized account access, affecting an estimated 40,000 customer accounts and carrying breach notification obligations in three states" states the business consequence first and the technical detail second, for anyone who wants it. "We have a CVSS 9.1 vulnerability in our OAuth implementation" is accurate and unusable by a board that isn't going to look up what CVSS 9.1 means mid-meeting. If a board member has to ask "what does that mean for us," the report failed before the discussion even starts. Connecting engineering spend and roadmap decisions to something the board governs: capital allocation and strategic risk. Framing a platform investment as "this reduces our customer onboarding time from six weeks to two, which our sales pipeline data shows is currently costing us an estimated 15 percent of qualified leads" ties the spend to a number the board already tracks. A roadmap slide organized by internal team names and sprint numbers. It's accurate to how the work is organized internally and meaningless to a board trying to understand what changes for the business and when. What a board needs to know here, distinct from an operational security review the CISO or security team runs separately. A small, stable set of metrics tracked over time: mean time to detect, mean time to remediate critical vulnerabilities, percentage of the environment covered by current compliance certifications, third-party and vendor posture (percentage of vendors with a current SOC 2 or equivalent), and current cyber insurance coverage, with any material incidents since the last meeting and the incident response postmortem attached if one occurred. A wall of green checkmarks with no trend line, no incident history, and no sense of how the organization compares to industry peers. A board cannot distinguish "consistently secure" from "we've never measured this rigorously enough to find a problem" without a track record and an external reference point to compare against. An increasingly standard board expectation, and one most technology leaders haven't built a repeatable format for yet. A short standing section covering what AI systems are in production, what's spent on them, and what governance controls are in place, referencing the AI Governance Map's control layers directly rather than reinventing the language each quarter. Boards are increasingly asking about this whether or not it's offered, and forward-looking boards are starting to ask about emerging technology risk more broadly, post-quantum cryptography readiness is now a live board discussion topic at some companies, not just AI. Treating an AI pilot as not board-relevant because it's "still experimental." If it touches customer data or a regulated decision, the board's risk oversight duty applies well before the system reaches full production, and finding out about it after an incident is worse than a modest early mention. Patterns that show up repeatedly enough to call out specifically rather than leave implicit in the sections above. Reporting activity (story points completed, deployments shipped) instead of outcomes (what changed for the business) Surprising the board with bad news in the meeting instead of a pre-brief to the chair or committee lead beforehand Treating every board update as a status report instead of occasionally using t

title: Build vs Buy
description: The criteria that decide a build-versus-buy debate, the differentiation test people misapply most often.
body: The criteria that decide it Score your own decision The differentiation test, asked honestly The maintenance question people skip The middle option nobody names: partner or extend Reversing the decision later Vendor risk beyond lock-in Signs the decision wasn't tested Most build-versus-buy debates get stuck arguing cost in isolation. Cost matters, but it's rarely the deciding factor once these are answered honestly. Score each criterion from the table above, 1 to 5, high meaning it leans build. Runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent anywhere or stored. The single most misapplied criterion, usually stretched to justify a decision already made for other reasons. A capability customers explicitly cite as why they chose you over an alternative, or one that materially changes your unit economics versus using a vendor. If you removed it, you'd lose deals or margin specifically because of its absence. "We want more control" or "the vendor's roadmap doesn't match ours exactly" are real preferences, but they aren't differentiation, and building an entire internal system to solve a preference is usually a worse trade than living with 90 percent fit from a vendor. Build decisions are evaluated on initial build cost far more often than on the ongoing cost of owning it for the next five years. Initial development time, initial infrastructure cost, time to first working version, the numbers that show up in a project proposal and are easy to estimate. Security patching indefinitely, keeping pace with a changing regulatory or integration landscape, the bus-factor risk when the one engineer who deeply understands it leaves, and the opportunity cost of the team's attention being split across build-and-maintain instead of focused on the actual differentiator. Build-versus-buy is usually presented as binary. A frequently better third option gets skipped. Buying a vendor platform for the undifferentiated 80 percent and building a thin, differentiated layer on top of it via the vendor's API or extension points, rather than building the whole stack from scratch or accepting 100 percent of the vendor's opinion. When the differentiation is narrow and specific (a particular workflow, a particular integration, a particular scoring model) rather than the whole domain. This is very often the actual right answer and gets dismissed early because the binary framing never surfaced it as an option. Build-versus-buy isn't necessarily a permanent choice. The sequencing of which comes first matters as much as the eventual answer. Start with a vendor to get to market fast. If the capability proves out as differentiation worth owning, build a deliberate replacement once you understand the real requirements from having lived with the vendor's version, rather than guessing at them upfront. Building something in-house "to stay flexible" before you know whether it's a differentiator usually produces a worse version of what a mature vendor already built, at a cost that vendor already amortized across many customers instead of just you. The framework above asks whether you can leave a vendor. It's an incomplete question on its own. Lock-in asks "can I leave." It's worth also asking what happens if the vendor leaves you: acquisition risk, a pricing change once you're dependent, a wind-down of the specific product you rely on. See Vendor Evaluation for scoring this directly. A string of individually reasonable buy decisions, each cleared on its own lock-in and exit-cost merits, that quietly concentrate several important capabilities behind the same vendor. A single vendor's bad quarter becomes every one of those capabilities' bad quarter at once. Patterns that show up when a build-versus-buy call was made to justify a preference rather than worked through honestly. Differentiation was asserted rather than tested against "would we lose deals or margin without this" No five-year total cost of ownership estimate exists for the build option, only the initial build cost The partner-or-extend middle option was never evaluated, only a binary build-or-buy framing No plan exists for reversing the decision later if the underlying assumption turns out wrong Vendor concentration across other decisions wasn't considered, only this one decision's lock-in risk in isolation

title: Business Case Calculator
description: A working NPV, IRR, and payback calculator for a multi-year technology investment, built on the same mechanics as the full business case workbook.
body: What the model produces Run the numbers What the pre-filled example represents Sensitivity: what happens if you're wrong Choosing a discount rate How business cases get gamed, and how to catch it Business case one-pager template Roll-up numbers from year-by-year cost and benefit inputs, the same structure as the full business case workbook: net present value, benefit-to-cost ratio, internal rate of return, and payback period. NPV: sum of discounted net cashflow across the analysis period Benefit-to-cost ratio: total benefits divided by total costs IRR: the discount rate at which NPV equals zero Payback period: when cumulative after-tax cashflow turns positive Verdict: a plain-language read on whether the case is strong, acceptable, or fragile NPV positive and B/C above roughly 1.5x reads as a strong case, NPV positive but B/C under 1.2x as worth funding but not a slam dunk, worth watching the sensitivity. These are illustrative reference points, not universal thresholds, your organization's actual bar depends on its cost of capital and risk appetite, and should be set deliberately rather than borrowed from this page. NPV negative at base case doesn't automatically kill an initiative with strategic value that doesn't show up in the numbers, but it does mean the strategic argument has to carry the case explicitly, not hide behind an inflated financial one. Enter total costs and benefits per year. Runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent anywhere or stored. Defaults are pre-filled with a representative example so you can see it work before entering your own numbers. The default numbers loaded above are a representative modernization program, not a template to copy blindly. Front-loaded implementation cost in Years 1 and 2, tapering to steady-state run cost by Year 3. Benefits ramp in behind it, typically 30 percent of steady-state value in Year 1, 70 percent in Year 2, full value from Year 3 onward, since adoption and realization lag the investment. A business case that assumes full benefit realization starting Year 1 is either describing a trivial change or overstating the case. Reviewers who've seen enough of these will discount an unramped benefit projection on sight. The single most common gap between a business case that survives real scrutiny and one that only looks solid under one set of assumptions. Run the same model at a pessimistic case, benefits 20 to 30 percent lower, costs 10 to 15 percent higher, before presenting the base case. If NPV still clears positive under the pessimistic scenario, the case is robust. If it only works at the base case, say so explicitly rather than letting the base case stand in for more confidence than the analysis supports. Presenting only the base case with no sensitivity shown. Either it was never tested, a real gap, or it was tested, the pessimistic case failed, and it quietly got left out of the deck, which a CFO who's seen enough of these will assume by default even without being told. The single input most likely to be pulled from thin air, and the one most likely to quietly determine the verdict. The return the capital could earn elsewhere, the company's actual cost of capital if it tracks one, or a hurdle rate leadership has explicitly agreed represents good enough for a technology investment. 8 percent shows up often as an illustrative default for an established company, but it's not a universal correct answer, your own cost of capital is company-specific and should replace it rather than be assumed to match it. A deliberately higher rate, 15 percent or more, is often used for early-stage or higher-risk bets specifically because the higher bar forces only the strongest cases through. Picking a lower discount rate because it makes more initiatives clear the bar, which quietly inflates the entire portfolio's apparent quality without anyone deciding to lower the standard. If the rate changes between two business cases with no stated reason, that's worth questioning before either number gets trusted. A handful of specific patterns account for most inflated cases. Worth knowing what to look for, whether reviewing someone else's case or checking your own honestly. Double-counted benefits. The same cost saving claimed by two different initiatives' business cases, each one looking stronger on its own than the two deliver combined. A skipped ramp. Full benefit value assumed from Year 1, which is either describing a trivial change or quietly overstating the case, covered above. Costs that stop at go-live. The build cost is modeled carefully; the run cost the initiative adds afterward, ongoing licensing, additional on-call load, incremental support burden, never makes it into the model at all. A quietly adjusted discount rate. The rate shifts from the standard used elsewhere in the portfolio, with no stated reason, until the number clears the bar. Drop the NPV, IRR, benefit-to-cost, and payback numbers from the calculator above straight into this one-pager, alongside the problem statement, strategic rationale, and risks a pure financial model doesn't capture. Markdown for pasting into your own docs system, or a formatted Word doc.

title: Working with the CEO
body: What the CEO needs from a CTO Telling the CEO no A worked example Founder CEO versus professional CEO When technology should be invisible, and when it's the strategy Handling a CEO who's miscalibrated in either direction Building trust before you need it Escalation and cadence, stated explicitly Signs the relationship is unhealthy Not a list of technical competencies. Four things a CEO can't get from anyone else on the team. The moment that defines the relationship more than any status update ever will. Arrive with the tradeoff already worked out, not just the refusal: "we can hit that date if we cut X, or hit full scope two weeks later, which do you want." A no with a stated alternative reads as judgment. A no with nothing behind it reads as an obstacle. A flat no delivered late, often after the CEO has already committed to the date externally, which turns a technical disagreement into a credibility problem for both people, and makes the next no much harder to deliver and to hear. What the mechanics above look like against a real, common scenario. The CEO wants to announce a launch date publicly at a conference six weeks out. The CTO's honest engineering estimate is ten weeks for the full feature set. Rather than a flat "we can't hit that," the CTO brings the tradeoff already worked out: a limited beta with three core features ships in six weeks, the full launch stays on the real ten-week timeline. The CEO announces the beta at the conference instead of the full launch. Engineering hits the beta date. The full launch ships on the timeline that was true from the start. Nobody's public credibility gets damaged, because what got promised matched what was deliverable, and the CEO had a real, positive announcement to make either way. The same relationship, shaped very differently depending on who's in the role. Often has deep intuitive product and technical instincts even without a formal technical background, and personal identity tied closely to the company. Disagreements can feel personal in a way they don't with a professional CEO. Technical credibility gets earned through demonstrated judgment over time, not through a title. Usually more process-oriented, expecting the same structured decision-rights model and reporting cadence used at previous companies. The relationship starts more transactional and earns trust faster through consistent, predictable execution rather than through personal rapport built up over years. Getting this posture wrong in either direction costs credibility. For most companies, most of the time, technology is an enabler. The goal is for the CEO to rarely have to think about it, and that quiet is a sign of health, not neglect, as long as it isn't masking a risk building underneath. When the technology is the competitive edge, what customers are buying is the technical capability, invisibility is the wrong posture. The CTO needs to be actively pushing technology into the CEO's strategic conversations, not staying quietly out of them. Two opposite failure modes, requiring opposite corrections. Treats every technical detail as something worth personally weighing in on. Give them a small, explicit set of decisions that warrant their attention, rather than either blocking them out entirely or letting them relitigate implementation details that don't. This is a translation failure, not a values failure. Find the specific business metric technology investment moves, and lead every conversation with that number, not with technical merit the CEO has no framework to evaluate. The high-stakes moments described above draw on a trust balance that has to be built somewhere else first. Regular, low-stakes contact, the weekly touchpoint described below, builds the trust that a high-stakes "telling the CEO no" moment later draws on. A CEO who's watched a CTO be right about smaller things repeatedly extends more benefit of the doubt when it matters most. The CTO only appears in the CEO's calendar when something's wrong, which means every interaction the CEO has with the CTO is colored by a problem, and trust never gets the chance to compound the way it does with regular, unremarkable contact. What should reach the CEO, and on what rhythm, shouldn't be reinvented every time something comes up. Escalate: a material change in risk, anything crossing a stated board-visibility threshold, and any commitment at risk of slipping, as early as it's known. Handle independently: implementation approach, internal architecture decisions, and day-to-day engineering management. A regular weekly touchpoint covers the practical items; a deeper monthly or quarterly conversation, tied to the broader operating cadence, covers strategy and portfolio; anything crossing an escalation threshold gets raised immediately, not saved for the next scheduled meeting. Patterns that show up when the CEO-CTO relationship has drifted, regardless of how well either person would describe it individually. The CEO learns about a material technology risk from someone other than the CTO Every technology conversation with the CEO is either a routine status update or a crisis, nothing in between The CTO can't name the one or two business metrics the CEO tracks Disagreements get resolved by whoever escalates loudest, not by a stated decision-rights model The CEO has stopped asking the CTO's opinion before making technology-adjacent decisions Most contact between the two only happens when something is already wrong

title: Cloud FinOps
description: Managing general infrastructure spend as a standing discipline, not a quarterly panic when finance asks why the cloud bill jumped.
body: Phases: one building block of a larger framework Where cost hides Rightsizing and idle elimination Reserved capacity and commitment strategy Tagging, showback, and chargeback Governance without becoming a bottleneck FOCUS: a shared billing language across clouds Crawl, Walk, Run, applied practically Score your own FinOps maturity Signs cost governance isn't working Cloud FinOps workbook Not an invented framework, these are the FinOps Foundation's own Phases, the industry body (under the Linux Foundation) that maintains the full FinOps Framework and the FOCUS billing specification referenced throughout this page. The complete framework also includes Principles, Personas, Domains and Capabilities, and Scopes, and the Foundation's current definition centers on maximizing the business value of technology spend broadly, not cloud specifically. Cloud, SaaS, AI, data center, and licensing are all recognized Scopes; this page covers the cloud infrastructure scope, which is why AI cost modeling gets its own page rather than folding into this one. The categories that consistently account for the largest share of avoidable spend, in roughly the order worth checking first. This is the Optimize phase in practice. The fastest money on the table, and the easiest to let slide once the first sweep is done. Automated shutdown for non-production environments outside business hours, utilization-based rightsizing recommendations reviewed monthly, and a default assumption that any resource untouched for 90 days gets flagged for a decommission decision rather than left alone indefinitely. Treating this as a one-time cleanup sprint instead of an ongoing practice. Six months after the sweep, utilization has drifted again and nobody's watching, because the tooling that found the savings the first time was never left running. Committing to reserved instances or savings plans locks in a discount and locks in a bet about future usage. Both halves matter. Commit only on the stable baseline, the usage level that's been consistent for at least six months, and use on-demand or short-term commitments for anything still growing or shrinking. Ladder commitment terms so not everything renews at once, which avoids a cliff where the whole discount structure needs renegotiating simultaneously. Overcommitting based on a growth projection that doesn't materialize, then paying for reserved capacity that sits unused, which is a worse outcome than paying on-demand rates for the same idle resource would have been. Cost visibility changes behavior. Cost invisibility guarantees nobody optimizes anything they can't see themselves accountable for. A mandatory tagging policy enforced at resource creation, not applied retroactively by a cleanup script, with showback reporting that puts each team's actual spend in front of that team monthly. Chargeback, where teams' budgets are directly debited, is a stronger lever but works only once tagging discipline is already solid. Rolling out chargeback before tagging is reliable, which produces disputed, inaccurate bills that teams learn to ignore rather than a credible signal they act on. Trust in the numbers has to come before the numbers carry financial weight. The tension every cost program eventually hits: enough control to prevent waste, not so much that provisioning something new takes a week of approvals. Guardrails over gatekeeping: budget alerts that trigger automatically, instance-size policies enforced by infrastructure-as-code rather than a manual review, and approval requirements reserved for large or unusual spend rather than every new resource. Most cost control should be invisible to an engineer working within normal bounds. A approval queue that becomes the default path for routine provisioning, which teaches engineers to over-request once to avoid asking twice, producing the exact oversizing the governance process was meant to prevent. The FinOps Foundation's second major contribution beyond the phase model, and the reason cross-cloud cost comparison stopped being a manual exercise. Before FOCUS (the FinOps Open Cost and Usage Specification), comparing a dollar of AWS spend to a dollar of Azure spend meant manually normalizing wildly different billing export formats, column names, and units. FOCUS is an open, vendor-neutral spec, now adopted by AWS, Microsoft, Google, and others, that puts every provider's billing data into the same shape. FOCUS standardizes the data format, not the underlying pricing or discount structures. A normalized bill still requires the same rightsizing and commitment discipline covered above; FOCUS removes the translation tax from the reporting layer, it doesn't remove the need for the practice itself. The FinOps Foundation's maturity model, stated concretely enough to assess against rather than claim. Crawl: tagging exists but is inconsistent, cost visibility is monthly and reactive, no forecasting. Walk: tagging enforced at creation, showback running, budgets set proactively, rightsizing is a recurring practice, not a one-time sweep. Run: chargeback in place, unit economics tracked (cost per customer or transaction), anomaly detection automated, cost is a first-class input to architecture decisions rather than an afterthought. Treating maturity as a label to claim rather than a description of what's happening. An organization that calls itself "Run" but can't answer what a single team spent last month is Crawl with better branding. Six capability domains from the FinOps Foundation framework, scored 1 to 5. Runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent anywhere or stored. Not exhaustive, but the patterns that show up consistently when a cost program looks good on paper and isn't changing behavior. title: Working with the CFO
body: What the CFO needs from a CTO Defending a number the CFO doesn't like When ROI framing doesn't fit, and saying so honestly The budget conversation before the budget conversation Capitalization and accounting realities worth understanding Signs the relationship is unhealthy Different from what the CEO needs. The CEO wants judgment and a point of view; the CFO wants numbers that survive scrutiny. The moment that determines whether the relationship is adversarial or productive going forward. Show the derivation, not just the conclusion. Walk through the specific assumption that, if changed, would change the number. Disagreement then becomes a conversation about one assumption, which is productive, instead of a vague sense that the number feels wrong, which isn't. Presenting a number as settled fact with no visible derivation. Any pushback then becomes a credibility fight rather than a disagreement about a specific input, and credibility fights are much harder to walk back than assumption disagreements. Forcing every investment into ROI language is a common, well-intentioned mistake that costs credibility over time. Infrastructure consolidation, a specific automation replacing manual work, a feature with a modeled revenue impact. These reduce cleanly to a number, and the CFO relationship is healthiest when that number is presented as exactly what it is. Security investment, reliability investment, and technical debt remediation reduce risk and avoid future cost; they rarely produce a clean, defensible ROI figure. Forcing one produces a number nobody believes, which costs more credibility than justifying the investment honestly on risk grounds instead. Where most CFO relationships go wrong: not in the numbers themselves, but in when the CFO first sees them. Bring the CFO the pre-ranked capital allocation priorities before the formal budget cycle starts, in a one-on-one setting. The first time the CFO sees the logic behind technology priorities should not be in a room with other executives present. The CFO's first exposure to how priorities were ranked happens live in the budget meeting itself, which makes every question feel adversarial even when it's just first contact with the reasoning. A CFO thinks in capex versus opex and amortization schedules. A CTO who understands the basics speaks the CFO's language instead of translating everything through an interpreter. Software development costs that qualify for capitalization under applicable accounting standards, versus costs that must be expensed immediately, materially change how a project's cost looks in a given quarter, independent of the project's actual value. Understanding this distinction, even at a high level, prevents a CTO from being caught off guard when a CFO cares more about the timing of a cost than its total, or pushes back on a schedule change that seems purely technical but carries a real capitalization consequence on the books. Patterns that show up when the CTO-CFO relationship has drifted into friction, regardless of how either person would describe it individually. Technology budget numbers get revised after the CFO has already committed them upward, more than once Every investment gets forced into ROI language regardless of whether it fits The CFO's first exposure to a priority ranking happens in a contentious budget meeting, not before it The CTO can't explain, at a basic level, why a project's cost is phased the way it is on the books Disagreements about a number become personal rather than staying focused on a specific stated assumption

title: The CTO Operating System
body: The five tiers Areas of responsibility Time allocation by company stage Why cadence beats reactive prioritization Why allocation should shift, not stay fixed Intended versus actual: where the time really goes The daily tier is smaller than it feels The quarterly reset is a reallocation decision, not a report The weekly tier: sync, not status The annual tier, done properly A worked week, illustrative Signs the operating cadence has decayed Each tier exists to protect a different kind of work from being displaced by the others. The failure mode at each tier is different too. The five tiers above answer when. This answers what, and where to go on this site for the full depth on each. Illustrative, not measured. The point is the direction of the shift, not the precision of any single number; treat these as a starting frame to check your own calendar against, not a target to hit exactly. M&A and diligence isn't in the table because it isn't a steady-state allocation; it spikes heavily during an active transaction regardless of stage and returns to near-zero afterward. The alternative to a stated cadence isn't no cadence, it's an implicit one where whoever's loudest wins. Separates urgent from important by giving each its own guaranteed slot, so a crisis doesn't consume the time that should go to the quarterly reallocation decision, and a quarterly review doesn't get treated with an urgency it doesn't warrant. Everything competes for attention at the same priority, and daily fires win every time by default. Long-horizon work, technical debt, succession planning, architecture evolution, never gets protected time because nothing forces it onto the calendar. The table above isn't three unrelated snapshots. It's one trajectory, and the shift itself has to be managed deliberately. Deliberately renegotiating your own time allocation at each real scaling milestone, a new engineering VP hired, a real architecture function stood up, a CFO relationship established, rather than letting the shift happen passively or resisting it out of habit. A CTO who keeps writing code and reviewing every pull request well past the point the org has outgrown that involvement becomes the bottleneck they used to prevent. A CTO who delegates architecture and technical judgment before the org has anyone ready to hold it leaves a real capability gap disguised as "scaling the team." Most CTOs, asked to describe their allocation, would sketch something close to the table above. Their calendar usually disagrees. An honestly audited calendar usually shows meetings and reactive interruptions consuming twenty to thirty percentage points more than intended, almost always stolen from technology strategy and hands-on deep work, the two categories with no urgent deadline forcing their own defense. The Thursday deep-work block described later on this page isn't a nice-to-have; it's the actual mechanism that defends strategy time from being silently eaten by whatever's urgent that particular week. Audit the real calendar quarterly against the intended allocation, not just a gut sense of how the time is going. Daily access to the CTO is available, which is exactly why the daily tier is the one most prone to creep. Only what can't wait: an active Sev1 or Sev2, a risk that just crossed a material threshold, an executive blocker stopping other work, a staffing emergency. If it could wait a week without real cost, it isn't a daily item. Status updates, routine decisions, and anything convenient get pulled into daily attention simply because the CTO is reachable, not because the item requires it. Once this starts, the daily tier stops protecting anything and just becomes the default channel for everything. The tier most likely to exist on the calendar and produce nothing. A real change: capital moved between horizons, a strategic assumption revisited and possibly overturned, an initiative killed. If nothing changed, the review didn't do its job, regardless of how thorough the discussion was. A calendar ritual summarizing the quarter that already happened, with no mechanism forcing a reallocation decision. The portfolio mix persists by inertia rather than by choice, and everyone leaves the room having confirmed what they already believed. The tier that runs most often and is therefore most at risk of becoming ritual rather than function. The weekly sync exists to make decisions that can't wait for the monthly review but don't rise to daily urgency: a hiring tradeoff, a scope cut, a risk needing more than one function's input. Attendees arrive having already read written updates, so the room's time goes to discussion and decisions, not readout. A round-robin status update where each function reports what it already reported in writing, consuming an hour that produces no decision. The actual decisions then happen in a separate, smaller, unscheduled conversation right after the "real" meeting ends, which quietly tells everyone the scheduled meeting wasn't where the real work happens. The tier most often compressed, and the one where compression costs the most. Weeks of groundwork before the offsite itself: the capital allocation review already run, the succession heatmap already updated, input already gathered from the people who'll be in the room. The offsite is for decisions and alignment, not first exposure to the material. A two-day offsite where strategy, budget, and org design all get worked out live in the room for the first time, producing decisions made on the spot that get quietly revisited and often reversed in the following weeks, once people have had time to think about material they were seeing for the first time under pressure.
