title: Technology Strategy During a Downturn
body: Bad cuts versus better cuts Don't confuse reducing spend with reducing value Communicating the cut without destroying morale What not to cut even under real pressure Sequencing the cuts, in order A worked example Rebuilding after the downturn ends Signs the cut was done badly Not every reduction in spend is equivalent. Some remove cost with almost no value loss; others remove cost by removing value. The two aren't the same thing, and the best cuts are the ones where they diverge most. Cloud rightsizing, duplicate SaaS tooling consolidation, and unused capacity elimination reduce spend with close to zero value loss. These should always be executed before anything with real value attached, and they're usually available in weeks, not quarters. An across-the-board percentage cut applied uniformly treats a duplicate analytics tool and a security control as equally expendable, which they are not, and guarantees the cut removes real value somewhere it didn't need to. How the reduction is explained matters almost as much as what's cut. Be specific about what's being cut and why, tied to the pre-ranked priority list, so the team understands this was a deliberate choice made against known criteria, not a panicked reaction to a number that arrived from finance. Vague, repeated "doing more with less" messaging with no specifics, which reads as either incompetence or dishonesty to the people doing the work, and erodes trust well beyond whatever the cut itself cost. Some categories aren't discretionary line items, whatever the topline number demands. Security, reliability, and necessary architectural remediation don't reduce cost when cut, they defer it at compounding interest. A downturn is exactly the moment the organization can least afford a preventable incident stacked on top of everything else already under pressure. If these categories appear on a cut list, the list needs to be rebuilt, not defended. Each step down this list is harder to reverse and costlier to trust than the one before it. Skipping ahead means paying the hardest cost first. Reversible, near-zero value loss: cloud rightsizing, duplicate tooling consolidation, unused capacity elimination Hiring freeze on non-critical roles: cheap, fully reversible, buys time to assess whether deeper cuts are needed Discretionary spend: travel, non-essential contractor engagements, training budgets not tied to a specific delivery commitment Innovation kill-criteria enforcement: stop bets that already failed the criteria set for them and hadn't been formally killed yet Structural headcount reduction: the last resort, the hardest to reverse, and the one that costs the most trust and future hiring ability What the sequencing above looks like against a real target, not just a list of categories. Target: an 18 percent reduction in a $12M engineering budget, roughly $2.16M. The headcount reduction still happens, but it's sized to $660,000, not the full $2.16M. Skipping straight to headcount to hit the number in one step would have meant a layoff roughly 3.3 times larger than what was necessary once the reversible options were exhausted first. The moment most organizations handle almost as badly as the cut itself. Revisit the cut list in the same order it was built. Some items, duplicate tooling, unused capacity, should stay cut permanently, since they were never real value to begin with. Reinstate only the categories that were value-reducing when cut. Automatically restoring every cut the moment budget allows, without asking whether the cut item was ever needed, which quietly re-inflates spend the organization had already proven it could operate without. Patterns that show up when a budget reduction was executed under pressure without the discipline this page describes. Cuts were applied as a uniform percentage rather than against a pre-ranked priority list Security or reliability budget was reduced specifically to hit a topline number The team was told to do more with less without specifics on what was deprioritized Innovation bets were cut without applying the kill criteria that should have already existed for them No one has revisited the cuts to confirm they didn't quietly become permanent once the downturn ended Headcount reduction happened before reversible options one through four were exhausted, not after

title: Transformation and Innovation
description: Two different problems that get called the same thing. Innovation is a selection problem, transformation is an adoption problem, and most failed initiatives are solving the wrong one.
body: Two different problems, one blurred word Diagnose which one you have The innovation stack: generating and selecting The transformation stack: adoption at scale Where this fits in the toolkit Before you call it a transformation The distinction that most conversations about "driving change" skip past. Before fixing anything, find out which problem is real, because the fixes don't transfer. The org executes reliably, ships on schedule, runs a tight operation, and keeps optimizing the same processes the same way. Nobody's proposing anything different, or the ideas that do surface never get a real evaluation against a kill criterion. More change management won't fix this. The gap is upstream, not enough real options ever reach a decision. The org has plenty of good ideas, pilots that work, proofs of concept that prove the concept, and none of them make it past the team or facility that built them. More AI pilots won't fix this. The gap is downstream, adoption, incentives, and the operating model never got built to carry a working idea past its origin point. Three real, citable pieces, not an invented framework, for the selection problem. Three real, citable pieces for the adoption problem, which is the one most technical leaders have the least formal training in. This page is the adoption layer the rest of the toolkit didn't have a name for. Run this before staffing an initiative as a transformation. If most of these are unanswered, it's still an innovation effort, and that's fine, just don't fund or staff it like the bigger thing. You can name the coalition, the specific people whose credibility will carry this past their own team, not just the executive sponsor who announced it You have a reinforcement plan for six months after launch, not just a training plan for week one The initiative is staffed and run differently from steady-state operations, not folded into the normal reporting cadence You know which ADKAR stage past pilots have died at, and it's not still Awareness You've distinguished whether the real gap is generating better options or getting existing good ones adopted, and you're not applying an innovation fix to an adoption problem or the reverse

title: Vendor Evaluation
description: A preview of the Vendor Evaluation Scorecard: weighted, multi-evaluator scoring across functional fit, security posture, financial stability.
body: Why multi-evaluator, not single-decision-maker Weighted scoring criteria Score a vendor Reference calls that surface something The lock-in question, asked before signing Contract terms that matter beyond price Negotiation leverage, and when to use it After signing: performance management, not filing it away Vendor evaluation scorecard The scorecard's real value isn't the criteria list, it's forcing the score itself to survive more than one perspective before it becomes a decision. Each stakeholder category, technical, security, finance, the actual end users, scores the vendor independently against the same criteria before anyone compares notes. Independent scoring first prevents the most senior or most vocal evaluator's opinion from anchoring everyone else's. The interesting result usually isn't the average score, it's the variance. A vendor scored a 4 by security and a 9 by the business sponsor is a conversation the scorecard forces to happen explicitly, before a contract is signed, rather than as a surprise after go-live. The categories that belong in every vendor evaluation, regardless of what's being bought, with the weighting varying by how critical and how sticky the vendor relationship will be. Score one vendor across the same six weighted dimensions from the table above. Runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent anywhere or stored. The full workbook supports multiple evaluators scoring independently and surfacing variance between them, which is where this framework earns its keep; this preview scores a single pass. The single highest-value, most consistently skipped step in vendor evaluation. Asking the vendor for a reference in a similar situation to yours (similar scale, similar use case), then asking that reference one specific question: "what would you do differently if you were choosing again today." That question surfaces real friction far more reliably than "are you happy with them." Accepting only the references the vendor's sales team hand-picked, and asking only satisfaction questions that have an obvious socially expected positive answer. This step becomes a formality that confirms nothing. Exit cost is far easier to evaluate honestly before a contract exists than after switching costs have already accumulated. What format can data be exported in, is there a contractual data portability clause, what's the actual notice period and any early termination penalty, and how much custom integration work exists that would need to be rebuilt for a different vendor. Discovering the actual exit cost during a renewal negotiation, at exactly the moment the vendor has the least incentive to make leaving easy and the most leverage to raise price, since they know switching now looks expensive. The number in the proposal is the easiest thing to negotiate. The clauses nobody reads carefully are usually what costs money later. Auto-renewal terms. How much notice is required to opt out, and does the notice window open before or after the price for the next term is disclosed. A short window that closes before the new price is revealed is a structural risk to you regardless of the vendor's intent, and worth negotiating out of the contract either way. Liability caps. What the vendor is on the hook for if their product causes a breach or an outage, often capped at fees paid, which can be a small fraction of the actual damage. SLA penalty structure. Whether missing the SLA produces a real, automatic credit or requires the customer to notice, document, and formally claim it, which most SLAs quietly rely on nobody doing. Most-favored-nation and price-lock clauses. Whether the contract protects against a price increase at renewal, and whether it's enforceable or just a stated intention. Leverage in a vendor negotiation is real but time-bound. Knowing when it exists changes what's worth pushing for. The vendor's fiscal quarter-end or year-end, when a sales rep needs the deal to close on their timeline, not yours. A genuine competitive alternative already evaluated, not bluffed. A multi-year commitment offered in exchange for a real discount, since the vendor values the certainty more than the marginal revenue from staying month-to-month. Threatening to walk with no real alternative lined up gets tested and lost quickly. A vendor negotiation team that's dealt with the bluff before will call it, and the next negotiation starts from a weaker position because the threat is no longer credible. A vendor evaluation that stops at the signature misses the half of the relationship that determines whether the choice was right. A standing quarterly business review for any vendor above a materiality threshold, tracking the same dimensions scored during evaluation, support responsiveness, uptime against the SLA, whether the integration is still fit for purpose. This is what turns the next renewal negotiation from a cold restart into a conversation grounded in a real track record. The scorecard gets built once, before signing, and never revisited. By renewal, eighteen months of drift in support quality or product direction is invisible, and the renewal decision gets made on inertia rather than on evidence, exactly the failure mode this whole page exists to prevent at the front end. The six weighted dimensions above in a fillable format, with per-dimension guidance and a place to log key risks and mitigations. title: Zero-Trust Maturity Preview
body: Six dimensions, scored independently Score your own environment Where to start, since you can't do all six at once Reading a real score pattern, not just the average Scoring honestly, and what to do with the result Compliance certification as a false signal of maturity Most organizations are unevenly mature across these six; that unevenness is itself the most useful output of the assessment, not a flaw in it. Rate each dimension 1 to 5 against the table above. This runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent anywhere or stored. Treating six dimensions as equally urgent is how effort gets spread thin everywhere and deep nowhere. Identity and access almost always comes first. Segmentation, detection, and even third-party risk all assume you can trust who's making a request in the first place; building micro-segmentation on top of standing broad access just adds complexity around a foundation that's still weak. Spreading effort evenly across all six dimensions produces slow, shallow progress everywhere and leaves the foundational dimension exactly as weak as it started, which is worse than concentrating effort where it compounds. What the six-dimension breakdown reveals when it's uneven, which it almost always is. Scores: Identity & access 2, Segmentation & blast radius 2, Detection & response 4, Vulnerability management 3, Third-party risk 2, Governance & culture 3. Average: 2.7. The diagnosis the average hides: strong detection sitting on top of weak identity and segmentation is a specific, dangerous pattern. This organization can see an attacker after they're already in, but the foundational controls that would have made getting in hard, or limited what they could reach once inside, are still weak. The instinct this score pattern usually triggers, buy more detection tooling since it's already the strongest area, is exactly backwards. More visibility into a wide-open environment doesn't reduce how wide open it is. Identity and segmentation need the next dollar, not detection. The assessment only has value if the scoring is honest, which is harder than it sounds when the person scoring it is also accountable for the result. Score against evidence, not intention. "We have a policy" is not Level 3 if the policy isn't followed; it's evidence of intent, not practice. Ask for the artifact (the actual access review log, the actual segmentation diagram, the actual vendor review record) before accepting a self-reported level. A Level 1 or 2 in any dimension is not itself an emergency; it's a prioritization input. Rank dimensions by business impact if that dimension fails, not by how uncomfortable the low score is, and fund the highest-impact gap first rather than the easiest one to fix. A frequent gap between what a certification confirms and what an organization assumes it confirms. SOC 2 or ISO 27001 confirms that defined controls existed and were followed during the specific audit period the certification covers, evaluated against a scope the organization itself proposed. That the scope covered every system that matters, that the maturity level is sustained rather than a point-in-time snapshot assembled for the audit, or that a novel attack pattern outside the certified controls would be caught. Treat certification as a floor, not a ceiling.
